column1: We discussed a case in the small group sessions about a patient who needed antibiotic premedication for a procedure, but did not want to comply with taking the antibiotics. The patient told his dentist that he would go to another dentist and not provide the medical information to the new dentist so he could be treated without the antibiotics. He told his original dentist not to communicate with the new dentist. Which of the following statements is TRUE:
column2: If the original dentist tells the new dentist that the patient needs antibiotics before treatment, this is consistent with the ethical principle of PATERNALISM.
column3: If the original dentist does not tell the new dentist that the patient needs antibiotics before treatment, this is consistent with the ethical principle of BENEFICENCE.
column4: If the original dentist does not tell the new dentist that the patient needs antibiotics before treatment, this is consistent with the ethical principle of NON-MALEFICENCE.
column5: If the original dentist does the procedure without premedication as the patient requested this is consistent with the ethical principle of NON-MALEFICENCE.
column6: If the original dentist does not tell the new dentist that the patient needs antibiotics before treatment, this is consistent with the ethical principle of patient AUTONOMY.

column1: The ADA has published a White Paper entitled The Ethics of Temporary Charitable Events. These events are sponsored by many organizations in order to increase access to dental care for patients that might not otherwise receive care. Which of the following scenarios is consistent with the ethical principle of NON-MALEFICENCE?
column2: These events are dependent on volunteers so it may be necessary to assign assisting duties to personnel who have not been trained or credentialed.
column3: Dentists may perform services that they do not routinely perform if an appropriate specialist is not available.
column4: Conditions at the site of the event may not allow for the same infection control techniques that are standard in the office setting. However as long as an effort is made to attempt to adhere to accepted standards, the event may be considered compliant.
column5: Discussions regarding treatment, including options and risks and benefits may be delegated to non-professionals in order to provide care to the largest number of people.
column6: Patients cannot be abandoned and must be provided with pertinent information and appropriate contact information so that they may receive necessary follow-up care.

column1: We discussed a case in the small group sessions about a suspected undocumented immigrant who was seeking care at a medical clinic. From a LEGAL standpoint, which of the following statements is TRUE?
column2: Doctors are obligated to report any crime, whether they witnessed it directly or their staff made them aware of it.
column3: Doctors are obligated to treat everyone.
column4: A duty to treat arises because a doctor has a pre-existing relationship with a patient or because in the circumstances the patient reasonably relies on the doctor's help
column5: “Good Samaritin” laws protect doctors who voluntarily decide to provide care to an individual in need, whether or not the doctor receives compensation for that care.
column6: If a patient lies to a doctor, the information they have provided (name, address, and any other data such as her health history and current complaint, etc.) is not protected from disclosure under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) <http://journalofethics.ama-assn.org/2016/03/pfor5-1603.html> and its implementing regulations.
column7: If a doctor suspects that a patient is attempting to commit insurance fraud, they can still bill the insurance provider, as long as they make a note about it in the patient's chart.

column1: We discussed a case in the small group sessions about a suspected undocumented immigrant who was seeking care at a medical clinic. In the opinion of the authors providing commentary about this case, from an ETHICAL standpoint, which of the following statements is NOT TRUE?
column2: If a patient has an acute life-threatening condition (for example, a stroke, respiratory distress, or ongoing blood loss), it is the physician's moral obligation to treat him or her, except under rare and extenuating circumstances-such as certain risk of dangerous exposure, injury, or death from attempting treatment.
column3: Working for free is a duty of all physicians.
column4: Doctors should leave prejudices at home when they enter the clinic or hospital.
column5: The demands of beneficence and the weight of the patient-doctor relationship can transcend the law, and a doctor could be morally justified if she or he chose not to comply with a specific law.
column6: Physicians are morally justified in “conscientiously objecting” to any law that requires them to act in contradiction to their professional duties to patients.

column1: We discussed a case in class where a faculty member selected students for a corporate dental group to interview for jobs. The following questions could be formulated: • Did the faculty member receive any compensation or perks for helping this company? • Did all of the students have the same exposure to this faculty member? • Did this help the school by giving some of its students a better chance of getting these good jobs than students from other schools? • Did students who might have otherwise had a chance at those jobs miss out because of the faculty member's intervention? • What criteria did the faculty member use in selecting the students for interviews? All of these questions are useful in assessing this case from an ethical standpoint.

column1: Which of the following statements is TRUE?
column2: Abuse of prescription medications and heroin addiction are two unrelated problems facing this nation.

column1: Which one of the following practices should be followed when prescribing opiates?
column2: A maximum of a two week supply of opiates should be prescribed after a routine dental procedure.
column3: It is appropriate to include three refills of opiates with the initial prescription after a dental procedure. If a patient request more opiates following these refills, the dentist should talk to them before giving additional refills.
column4: NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen, Motrin, Advil) and/or acetaminophen can often be used to provide adequate pain relief following dental procedures so that opiates may not be necessary.
column5: Opiates may only be prescribed for someone who is not a patient of record in emergency situations where they are in otherwise uncontrollable pain.
column6: Opiates may be safely prescribed to patients taking any drugs, whether or not those drugs were prescribed to them.

column1: Attachments to pain prescriptions may be a useful tool in reducing prescription drug abuse. The attachment should include all of the following, EXCEPT:
column2: Your unused pain medication is a potential threat to family and friends.

column4: Properly dispose of unused medications, rather than keeping them for that “just in case” moment.
column5: Do not flush medications down any drains, as medication may find its way into the water supply.
column6: Make sure that anyone you share this medication with understands that it MAY impair them and that they should not drive or operate heavy machinery while taking this medication.

column1: When providing dental care to patients who are in Recovery, which of the following statements is NOT TRUE?
column2: Avoid mood altering drugs, if at all possible.

column6: If they are receiving medications to help them with their abuse problem, such as methadone or buprenorphine maintenance, they cannot have problems with the use of opiates.

column1: Patients below the age of 18 are generally considered minors and their parent or guardian is required to provide consent for treatment. column2: In NY, patients must be 13 years-old or older to legally provide consent when the treating doctor believes that they have the emotional and cognitive ability to function as an adult.
column3: In all states in the U.S., patients must be 13 years-old or older to legally provide consent when the treating doctor believes that they have the emotional and cognitive ability to function as an adult.
column4: In NY, patients must be 16 years-old or older to legally provide consent whenthe treating doctor believes that they have the emotional and cognitive ability to function as an adult.
column5: In all states in the U.S., patients must be 16 years-old or older to legally provide consent when the treating doctor believes that they have the emotional and cognitive ability to function as an adult.
